statement: Streets form a square grid. Jo walks from home to a library 5 blocks east and 3 blocks north, always going east or north along the streets. She must pass the fountain at the corner 2 blocks east and 2 blocks north of her home. How many different routes can she take?

choices.misconception: I counted only the routes from home to the fountain and forgot the part from the fountain to the library.
I added the 6 routes to the fountain and the 4 routes from it, instead of multiplying.
I counted the routes that miss the fountain instead of the routes that pass it.
I counted all routes from home to the library, forgetting that she must pass the fountain.

hints: Split the walk into two parts at the fountain.
Count the routes from home to the fountain, and from the fountain to the library, separately. Any first part can be followed by any second part.
Home to fountain is 2 east and 2 north: 6 routes. Fountain to library is 3 east and 1 north: 4 routes.

solutions.reliable: From home to the fountain Jo walks 2 blocks east and 2 north in some order: EENN, ENEN, ENNE, NEEN, NENE, NNEE, which is 6 routes. From the fountain to the library she walks 3 east and 1 north, and the one north block can come 1st, 2nd, 3rd or 4th, so 4 routes. Each first part can be joined to each second part, giving 6 × 4 = 24 routes. The transferable idea: a route forced through a point splits into two independent parts, and the counts multiply.

whyOnTest: Grid paths through a checkpoint test whether a student splits the walk and multiplies the two counts rather than adding them.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
